item.title: Daddy Yankee Gives Biggie His Flowers For Inspiring Reggaeton
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Daddy Yankee credited Biggie and dancehall on Track Star and said he coined reggaeton's name in 1992, revisiting its roots.
item.content:encoded:
Daddy Yankee credited Biggie and Jamaican dancehall as influences on his music during “Track Star,” where he also claimed he came up with reggaeton’s name in 1992.

During an interview with Jack Coyne, the Puerto Rican star recognized The Notorious B.I.G. and Shabba Ranks as the artists who shaped him. Calling Biggie a formative influence, he said, “he’s a great legend and he inspired me a lot.”

He also named Super Cat, Buju Banton and Beenie Man among the Jamaican artists who influenced Puerto Rican musicians.

Yankee’s claim concerned naming reggaeton. The sound grew out of a wider movement of rappers, DJs and Caribbean music.

A 2023 history published by El País placed Yankee’s use of the word on a DJ Playero recording around 1991 or 1992. Playero recalled the moment as something that happened while they were making a song, rather than a planned announcement of a new genre.

“Nobody knows, neither him nor me. It was part of a song we were putting together,” Playero said when asked why Yankee used the word, calling it “a pure coincidence.”

That history also described an early scene built through cassette sales on Puerto Rican streets. DJ Adam Avilés recalled that the music was called underground before it had a place on radio, television or store shelves.

DJs recorded young rappers over the beats, helping the sound circulate outside the usual industry channels.

Scholar Petra Rivera-Rideau’s essay for the Library of Congress traced underground’s development to Puerto Rican DJs in the early 1990s.

Pioneers such as DJ Negro and Playero “combined sounds from US hip-hop, Jamaican dancehall, and Panamanian reggae en español” with ideas of their own, she wrote.

Yankee had described that connection in his 2007 interview with AllHipHop. Asked whether he considered himself a reggaeton or Hip-Hop artist, he answered, “Both. Both of them.”

“I started it in the Latin world, was as a Hip-Hop artist…Latin Hip-Hop artist. Then, Playero, the reggaeton godfather, introduced me to reggae music and dancehall music. He taught me how to get down [in] the reggae world like 13 years ago, 14 years ago. So thanks to him, I discovered reggaeton music. So I place myself as a Latin Hip-Hop artist and a reggaeton artist, Daddy Yankee told AllHipHop.com.

On “Track Star,” Yankee also credited New York as “the biggest bridge to reggaeton” and identified Héctor Lavoe’s “El Cantante.” “I’m a salsa boy, man, from the heart,” he said.

His own crossover became part of the historical record: “Gasolina,” from his 2004 album Barrio Fino, entered the Library of Congress’ National Recording Registry in 2023. Rivera-Rideau described how the song reached American rap and pop radio, MTV and BET, carrying reggaeton well beyond its early underground audience.

item.title: Positive K Finds A Purpose Bigger Than Rap: Caring For Mom With Alzheimer’s
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Positive K shared how caring for his mother, who has Alzheimer's, changed his life and why caregivers need a team.
item.content:encoded:
Positive K has made caring for his mother his priority as she lives with Alzheimer’s disease.

The rapper discussed looking after his mother, Julie, in an Atlanta News First interview published October 29. She has had the disease for years, with changes to her movement, speech and ability to think.

“This is my assignment in life,” he said.

There have been hard days, but he has also enjoyed choosing outfits for her. He credited the Alzheimer’s Association Georgia Chapter with answering when he sought help from relatives and others.

“It really involves everyone, and that is why you need a team,” Positive K said of caregiving.

He said the experience went beyond music into his personal relationships and changed how he made decisions. He felt he had grown as a son and as a person. He still hoped to return to music full time, taking what he learned from caring for his mother with him.

His creative work has also included stand-up comedy. In a 2023 AllHipHop exclusive, the MC spoke about opening for Mike Epps in 2021 and learning to work different rooms. He described earning his place among comedians rather than relying on his rap fame.

The need for help comes into focus during November, National Family Caregivers Month. The Alzheimer’s Association says nearly 13 million Americans provide unpaid care for someone with dementia. It reports that 59 percent of dementia caregivers experience high emotional stress and 38 percent experience physical stress tied to their care duties.

For families looking for the kind of team Positive K described, the Georgia chapter offers free support groups. Caregivers can join by phone, video or in person, with trained facilitators leading the sessions. There are also groups for people in the early stages of dementia, giving families more than one way to find others facing similar changes.

The association’s free helpline, 800-272-3900, is open around the clock. Callers can speak with someone about local resources or get emotional support and crisis assistance. Conversations are confidential, with bilingual staff and interpreters making help available in more than 200 languages.

item.title: Hip-Hop DJs Turn Election Day Into A Nearly 5,000-Stop Gig
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Hip-Hop DJs will play outside polling places November 3 as DJs at the Polls adds Tampa and Kansas to its national effort.
item.content:encoded:
Hip-Hop DJs have a different kind of Election Day booking on November 3: polling places, a national effort built by a former BET “Rap City” worker.

DJs at the Polls will make its first appearance in the Tampa area at 26 polling locations in Tampa and elsewhere in Hillsborough County, WUSF reported. Founder Anton Moore developed the idea while working on “Rap City”, bringing his experience around rappers and DJs into voter engagement.

Moore founded the nonpartisan initiative in Philadelphia in 2009. Legendary Philly spinner DJ Diamond Kuts serves as DJ Recruitment Lead.

Its mission puts music to work around a civic task: encouraging people to participate by making Election Day feel like a community celebration.

The organization is a fiscally sponsored project of Focus for Democracy Fund, a nonprofit.

This year, about 2,000 DJs will perform at nearly 5,000 polling locations in 24 states, KCUR reported. Kansas is another first-time stop for the organization, with 18 voting sites in Kansas City, Kansas, and 28 locations in the Wichita area on the schedule.

Those gigs pay $500 per set. The assignments come with rules: DJs cannot play offensive music or use their sets to push a political affiliation. Moore said performers receive training on the guidelines, including the ban on profanity.

On the organization’s website, past participant DJ World Wide Waxx described what the work felt like from behind the equipment: “The people enjoy it and they thank you a lot for even being there.”

item.title: Yella Beezy Trial Examines Limits Of $100 Bill Tracking
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Yella Beezy's jury heard how two $100 bills were traced to banks and why those records cannot identify who later held the cash.
item.content:encoded:
Yella Beezy‘s murder-for-hire trial heard testimony Wednesday from Federal Reserve director Joseph Catania about how newly printed $100 bills are tracked through the banking system.

Catania, who has worked at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York for 13 years, explained how shipping records document the initial distribution of new currency.

When banks order newly printed cash, the bills arrive in sequential order with unique 11-character serial numbers. Federal Reserve staff scan package barcodes to record the serial-number ranges, receiving bank and distribution date.

“For brand new currency, $100 bills, the Federal Reserve cash office that pays out that currency will keep a record of which bank that currency is to go to and what day and what year,” Catania testified. “When currency is brand new, it is in sequential numbered order. Each banknote contains an 11 character serial number of letters and numbers that should be unique to that note.”

Catania also explained a key limit: those records do not track individual bills after they enter the banking system or identify who holds them later.

Customers can withdraw the money, spend it and return it to circulation without the Federal Reserve recording each transaction.

“So, what we can do if you have a $100 bank note and it has a serial number, you provide us that serial number, we can tell you which bank that note got paid out to and when that note got paid out to that bank,” Catania said. “The limitation being we can’t track the bill and who it goes to, whose hand end user it ends up in, where it’s spent, how it’s used, anything like that.”

Prosecutors presented two $100 bills as evidence in the case. One bill, bearing serial number LF 8085 1614B, was traced to a Bank of America branch in Hialeah, Florida, where it was distributed in 2014.

The second bill, bearing serial number MK 69320001, was traced to One World Bank in Dallas, where it was distributed in June 2020.

Prosecutors allege Yella Beezy, whose legal name is Markies Conway, paid $40,000 to have Dallas rapper MO3, Melvin Noble Jr., killed on Interstate 35 in 2020. He has pleaded not guilty in the MO3 murder case.

The testimony outlined what the Federal Reserve’s records can establish about the bills and where that evidence stops.

Those records identify the banks that first received the new currency but cannot, on their own, establish who later handled it or how it was spent.

item.title: Karen Bass Becomes A Rap Target In Nithya Raman’s Paid Diss Track
item.dc:creator: AllHipHop Staff
item.description: My Favorite Color took aim at Karen Bass in a paid campaign diss track as Nithya Raman pushed to become Los Angeles mayor.
item.content:encoded:
My Favorite Color took a paid shot at Karen Bass as Nithya Raman’s campaign brought a diss track into the Los Angeles mayoral race.

My Favorite Color is Anthony Willis, a Los Angeles rapper from Pittsburgh. The rapper posted the video with a caption saying Raman’s campaign paid for it. The song ran just under two minutes and attacked the incumbent mayor’s handling of homelessness and the January 2025 wildfires.

“Bro, I pinky promise Karen Bass ain’t your savior,” he rapped. The song also joked about the lawsuit involving rapper Ovrkast and OutKast while questioning Bass’ performance as mayor.

The lyrics criticized Bass’ meeting attendance and mocked her supporters. The song put a Los Angeles rapper into a campaign that had already drawn support from some well-known film and television actors.

The rapper stood by the message Monday morning. Asked for comment, My Favorite Color told KTLA, “What has Karen Bass done for y’all?” He also encouraged Angelenos to vote.

Bass had already faced Raman over the same issues at their October 13 debate. The two were once allies, but their dispute over city leadership included who bore responsibility for homelessness spending and how the mayor handled an emergency.

Raman argued that homelessness had risen despite the money spent and accused Bass of being absent. Bass defended her Inside Safe housing program, pointing out that Raman had chaired the committee responsible for the issue and had voted to approve the spending.

The mayor also addressed being out of the country when the Palisades fire began. “I am so profoundly sorry that I was not in my city, when my city needed me,” Bass said during the earlier debate. Raman promised to be present during the next emergency.

On Bass’ side, Samuel L. Jackson backed her in an October 25 campaign video, defending her work on homelessness. He argued that responding to problems across an entire city was harder than running a single district.

Anthony Anderson also appeared in a campaign video supporting Bass and highlighted her work on film and television tax credits.

Los Angeles voters choose between Bass and Raman on November 3.

item.title: Pete Rock Backs Tru Soul’s First Signee With Full Album
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Pete Rock's first Tru Soul Records signee AMXXR is readying DopeBoySoul, a full album with the producer due December 4.
item.content:encoded:
Pete Rock is backing his label Tru Soul Records’ first signee, AMXXR, with a full album titled DopeBoySoul, set for December 4, 2026.

The Mount Vernon, New York rapper has worked with Pete Rock for years. The legendary producer will craft their next project entirely, extending a partnership that already includes the mixtape 21 Grams: Worth Its Weight In Soul.

The first single, “What You Gonna Do,” arrived October 23, giving listeners a lead track ahead of the December release.

AMXXR described the song as a reflection on faith and growth, calling it a record about “seeing the blessing in the pressure, trusting God’s timing and becoming better than your last version.”

Tru Soul also has a catalog beyond AMXXR, with Pete Rock’s instrumental collection Return Of The SP1200 as the label’s debut release. That project gathered beats he made as a teenager in Mount Vernon and included additional scratches from J. Rocc of the Beat Junkies.

Pete Rock’s work with another MC has since earned Grammy attention.

His Common collaboration The Auditorium Vol. 1 was nominated for Best Rap Album at the 2025 ceremony. As AllHipHop reported, the pair also received a Best Rap Performance nomination for “When the Sun Shines Again,” featuring Posdnuos.

Before the new album arrives, AMXXR is scheduled to share a bill with Pete Rock and Slum Village at Brooklyn Bowl Philadelphia on November 5. Rap veteran Hezekiah, Vice Soulectric and Cosmo Baker are also on the lineup for the 8 P.M. show.

item.title: Chance The Rapper’s SocialWorks Sets 11-Site Chicago Winter Drive
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Chance the Rapper's SocialWorks announced a winter supply drive with 11 Chicago collection sites and a January 10 deadline.
item.content:encoded:
Chance the Rapper‘s SocialWorks is asking Chicago residents to help stock 11 collection sites with winter supplies for people experiencing homelessness.

The nonprofit’s ninth annual Warmest Winter clothing drive will run from November 2, 2026, through January 10, 2027. Its wish list includes coats, jackets, scarves, gloves, hats, blankets and socks, either new or gently used.

Toys can also be new or gently used. Hygiene products must be new, including soap, deodorant, toothpaste and toothbrushes. Diapers, baby clothes and other baby essentials are welcome. Food and canned goods are not accepted.

“For nine years, Warmest Winter has brought Chicagoans together around a simple belief: everyone deserves warmth, dignity, and care,” SocialWorks said in its announcement.

The effort has drawn support from Chicago students and adult donors. During the previous winter season, Owen Elementary’s Class of 2026 collected eight bags for SocialWorks’ closet, Chicago Public Schools said in a February update.

The Ashburn school’s donations included shoes, cold-weather clothing, hygiene supplies and baby items. It was Owen’s third year taking part in the drive.

Warmest Winter also reaches beyond the annual collection period. SocialWorks describes it as a year-round effort for people facing homelessness and extreme hardship, with volunteer work and outings alongside its clothing drive and holiday event.

Its SocialThreads clothing pantry, run in collaboration with Chicago’s Department of Family and Support Services, offers free clothes, toys and hygiene supplies. People can choose items that fit their own needs and style.

Chance’s winter fundraising goes back more than a decade. In January 2016, AllHipHop covered his Warmest Winter campaign, which raised $100,000 to help provide coats for Chicago residents experiencing homelessness.

This May, the rapper was among those honored at TIME’s philanthropy impact dinner in New York City. He spoke there about the responsibility that comes with that recognition, calling for continued care for children.

“We’re continuing to look out for the children, that we are building a world that’s safe for them,” Chance said at the May 21 event.

For this season’s donations, SocialWorks’ announcement includes a collection-site map. Donors should check building access and holiday hours before heading out.

item.title: Ice-T Dismisses Parenting Critics With Two Blunt Words
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Ice-T and Coco Austin have faced years of scrutiny over raising Chanel, whose school milestones have also played out online.
item.content:encoded:
Ice-T told E! News “F–k ’em” when asked about parenting critics at Heidi Klum’s Halloween party.

The rapper and actor has spent years defending how he and Coco Austin raise Chanel while sharing parts of their family life online. He compared their household to another famous family’s and pushed back against treating all parents the same.

“We’re like the Osbournes. We have a different dynamic in our house. But it’s not harmful. That’s the main thing. It’s us,” he said in a previous interview.

Chanel is his youngest child and his only child with Austin, following his older daughter, LeTesha and son, Tracy Jr., from previous relationships.

The couple’s choices drew criticism in 2022 when Austin shared footage of Chanel bathing in a kitchen sink before heading to a fashion show.

The child was six at the time, and Austin explained that using the sink helped her get ready faster.

She defended the decision in an interview with Page Six, telling the outlet, “Everything I do, people have got to say something about it.”

That year also brought complaints about Austin using a stroller for Chanel, adding another dispute over a routine family outing to the public discussion.

An earlier argument centered on Austin breastfeeding Chanel at five, which she described as a source of comfort and closeness for her daughter.

“Chanel still likes my boobs. It’s a big bonding moment for a mother and your child,” Austin told Us Weekly in 2021.

Austin said Chanel also ate meals and sometimes wanted to nurse, explaining that she would let her daughter decide when to stop.

The public family updates have also included school milestones, with Austin sharing Chanel’s fourth-grade graduation picture on Instagram in June and reflecting on time passing.

She joked about gathering mothers for a group where they could share that feeling over coffee or tea, even suggesting tequila as another option.

“To all the moms who blinked and suddenly their little baby is graduating another grade-I’m right there with you,” Austin wrote.

Chanel, who was born November 28, 2015, will celebrate her 11th birthday later this month.

item.title: Ja Rule Rethinks Slowing Down After Alicia Keys’ Clive Davis Tribute
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Ja Rule weighed more time with his family before a tribute to Clive Davis gave him a fresh view of his future in music.
item.content:encoded:
Ja Rule reconsidered slowing down his career after Alicia Keys’ tribute to Clive Davis made him see another path for his next chapter.

In a Jerusalem Post interview, the Hip-Hop veteran explained how hearing about Davis’ late-career comeback changed his plans for the years ahead.

“I learned a lot there. I left feeling truly inspired,” he said of Davis’ funeral and the tributes he heard there.

At 50, Ja Rule had been weighing time with his children and granddaughter Bella against the pace that kept him working through their childhoods.

Keys’ account of Davis starting again at 67 gave him a different way to think about age and the years ahead.

“And at that moment, I realized I wasn’t done yet,” he said, recalling how her tribute changed his thoughts that day.

Davis’ Manhattan funeral took place June 29, with Ja Rule among the artists gathered at Central Synagogue to honor the executive.

Alicia Keys, Dionne Warwick, Barry Manilow and Stevie Wonder also attended, while Bruce Springsteen spoke and Jennifer Hudson sang at the private service.

The ceremony was streamed for the public, bringing together performers whose careers crossed different styles but shared a link to Davis’ work.

Ja Rule’s concerns about time with family follow an earlier public adjustment to his new role as a grandfather and how he announced it.

He had revealed the pregnancy to Sherri before acknowledging that he might have spoken before his family intended.

“Big mouth, big papa. Spilled all the beans,” he joked.

Ja Rule also connected his desire to be present for his family to growing up without his father, whose absence shaped his approach.

Asked what he wanted to achieve in that role, he answered, “Being the best grandfather that I could be.”

His trip also put him back before a live audience, with an October 29 set at Hangar 11 drawing on songs including “Mesmerize” and “New York.”

item.title: Nelly Turns To Ashanti For Cash After Losing At Spades To Michael Jordan
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Nelly recalled asking Ashanti for cash after he and his brother lost a spades game against Michael Jordan and Charles Oakley.
item.content:encoded:
Nelly had to ask Ashanti for money after a spades game against Michael Jordan left him short on cash, with his wife there to see him lose.

The rapper recalled the night on “7PM in Brooklyn with Carmelo Anthony,” where he joined Anthony, Monica and Kaz. The episode was released October 30 in the United States.

He and his younger brother had teamed up against Jordan and Charles Oakley. Nelly remembered winning early, then talking trash. Ashanti’s presence helped encourage the boasting, he explained, before the game turned in the other team’s favor.

“He did it in front of my woman,” Nelly said before asking Ashanti, “lost a lot of money that night. Babe, what you got in that pocket?” he recalled.

Oakley reminded him that he had warned him about talking too much. Still, Nelly described the experience warmly, recalling how much he enjoyed being welcomed into that circle.

The rapper and Jordan have both held stakes in the Charlotte Bobcats. AllHipHop reported in July 2004 that Nelly had become a part-owner alongside Bob Johnson. Jordan later joined the ownership group, then moved to take control of the team.

The NBA approved his purchase of a controlling interest on March 17, 2010. At the time of his investment, Nelly described owning part of the franchise as one of the biggest achievements of his career.

Fans will soon get more of Nelly and Ashanti’s life together through the second season of “Nelly & Ashanti: We Belong Together,” which premieres November 19 on Peacock. They are raising their toddler son Kareem, known as KK, while managing work that often takes them away from each other.

“We’re both on tour at different times, being in different places,” Nelly explained in the season’s trailer.

The series will also follow their decisions about showing their son on social media and the demands of a blended family.

Ashanti works on new recordings while Nelly deals with the physical strain of touring. Ashanti also moves between St. Louis and New York City as she balances motherhood, music and performances.
